textbook_pages.title: Our year of maths
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text:
Try. Check.
Explain.

Mr Aliyu: Our class in Gombe is making a maths trail for another class. We will remember, try and check.
Aishatu: I will build the box stations, and wait while we check.
Adamu: Everyone needs a fair turn.
Grace: A smudge need not end our work. I can retry.
John: Keep the stations in reach. Let me solve the puzzle before you tell me.

textbook_pages.title: Number station
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu puts 4 counters down. He touches each once: 1, 2, 3, 4. Then he adds 2: 5, 6. So 4 + 2 = 6. Grace checks by moving each counter once.
Try together. Put 3 counters down. Add 2. Count them together. Explain how you avoid counting one twice.
Remember the method. Then try the matching station in your workbook. An adult can read the words aloud. Use safe large objects at a reachable table.

textbook_pages.title: Part station
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu puts 7 counters down. He moves 3 away. 4 remain: 7 - 3 = 4. He checks 3 + 4 = 7. Adamu makes sure each friend can see.
Try together. Put 8 counters down. Move 2 away. Say the remaining number. Check by putting the parts together.
Remember the method. Then try the matching station in your workbook. An adult can read the words aloud. Use safe large objects at a reachable table.

textbook_pages.title: Compare and shape station
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu aligns the ends of two safe strips. One extends farther: it is longer. Aishatu waits while John feels the aligned ends. Then they fold one paper circle into two equal matching parts: each is a half.
Try together. Use two safe strips. Align one end. Say which is longer, shorter or equal. Fold a paper circle into two equal matching parts. Explain why the parts are halves.
Remember the method. Then try the matching station in your workbook. An adult can read the words aloud. Use safe large objects at a reachable table.

textbook_pages.title: Check the trail
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text: Recall: Explain one way to check a count and one way to check a subtraction. Tell a friend without looking back.

Need help? Mr Aliyu starts with 2 counters and adds 1. Touch each once. Put the model away. Now try 2 and 2 independently, without a hint. John moves the counters; Grace checks. Aishatu waits and Adamu invites everyone to explain.
Try afresh: Start with 6 counters. Add 3. How many? Check it another way. The friends test each station, repair a wrong label, then open their reachable maths trail. Everyone can take a turn.

textbook_pages.title: Show what you remember
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text: At the end of each suggested term, try its workbook check. An adult reads the words. First explain aloud, then try the objects, then write or draw. Use an exercise book if needed.
Choose a quiet short session. Take a break when needed. Try on your own first. Tell the adult if you need help. There is time to learn again.
After the whole-year check, share one method you remember. The trail is ready because the friends checked their work, helped fairly and corrected mistakes.

textbook_pages.title: A pretend chat about maths
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text:
Ask clearly.
Check the answer.

Mrs Binta: Our Gombe class will act out printed pretend chats. No phone, computer or internet is needed. AI is short for artificial intelligence. It is a computer tool made by people. It uses patterns learned from many examples to make replies. It is not a person and has no feelings.
Aishatu: Can an answer be wrong?
Mrs Binta: Yes. We use our own maths to check. An adult reads the pretend AI lines.

textbook_pages.title: Catch a pretend mistake
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text: All chat lines on these pages are invented examples, not real AI replies.

Mrs Binta asks: How many counters are here?
Pretend AI — WRONG: There are five counters.

Grace: Let us touch each counter once.
Mrs Binta: One, two, three, four. There are four, not five.
Adamu: We corrected the pretend answer fairly.
Try together. Point once to each counter. Say the correct number. Explain the mistake. Never trust a reply just because it sounds sure.

textbook_pages.title: Ask a clear maths question
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text:
John: Let me try first.
John asks: I have three counters. I add two. How many altogether?
Pretend AI: Five.
Mrs Binta: Use real counters to check: three and two make five.
Your turn: Tell an adult a clear question about two counters and one more. The adult reads this invented reply: Three. Check with counters. Explain your check.
Keep private things private. Use made-up maths examples. Do not put names, addresses, passwords or photos into a chat. Ask a trusted adult for help. No one needs to share private information here.

textbook_pages.title: Think, check and explain
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Speak, point or use your exercise book.

elements.text:
Aishatu: I can wait while we check.
Pretend question: How many counters are below?
Pretend AI — WRONG: Four.
Try on your own. Point once to each counter. Say the correct answer. Explain why the pretend reply is wrong. Tell an adult; write or draw in your workbook or exercise book.

Need a smaller step? Check two real counters with the adult, then put the model away and try a new set of three independently, without a hint. Recall: ask clearly; keep private things private; check with your own maths.
John explains the check. Grace repairs the card. Adamu gives everyone a turn. Mrs Binta says: Our trail ends with careful thinking. A computer answer never replaces your checking.

elements.text: Suggested terms and checks are editorial pacing, not an official scheme. Term one revisits Chapters 1–5; term two Chapters 6–12; term three Chapters 13–19. Review stations sample earlier learning. Every historical objective remains linked to its full chapter teaching and checks in the objective ledger, not certified by these small mixed checks.

Read instructions aloud without supplying a mathematical answer. Record separately: oral explanation, written/numeral response, practical action; unaided, after neutral rereading, or after teaching/support. Record not assessed when resources or access are missing. Arrange reachable safe materials; accept speaking, pointing and moving objects. Teacher may explain in pupils’ familiar language; no translations are asserted here.

After an error, identify the method: double counting, unaligned ends, unequal parts, place-value confusion. Return to the matching chapter model with smaller real sets. Recheck with different values after support, then again after several days without the model. Record the exact task, response, help and date. Do not infer mastery of untested objectives or outcomes.

adult_pages.title: Fresh rechecks and later recall
adult_pages.subtitle: For the adult. Pupil responses are oral, practical or on separate paper.

elements.text: Revision: after support with 2 + 1, use 2 + 2 (4); a few days later use 4 + 3 (7). Ask how the pupil checked. For subtraction support use 4 take away 1 (3), then 5 take away 2 (3); delayed use 6 take away 2 (4). For parts use a fresh paper shape; check equal parts, not only the word half.

Term checks: revisit the chapter linked to each error. Fresh/recheck pairs: T1 count 4 then 7 and read 7 then 6; T2 3 + 2 = 5 then 4 + 3 = 7; T3 pretend 2 + 2 = 4 then 5 + 1 = 6. Recheck the practical method with different strips/objects. After several days use new values or new materials; record what was actually observed.

AI: after the supported two/three counter steps, delayed recall uses five real counters: an adult reads the invented wrong reply ‘six’. Ask the pupil to find and explain the correct five. Separately ask what to keep private; no disclosure. These are printed simulations only. No real device, platform, account or live output is used. Correct answers alone do not establish privacy understanding.

adult_pages.subtitle: For the adult. Pupil responses are oral, practical or on separate paper.

elements.text: AI: artificial intelligence, a computer tool made by people that uses patterns learned from many examples to make replies; not a person. Simulated: acted out or invented. Private: information to keep to yourself and a trusted adult. Verify: check for yourself. Existing chapter word lists and complete answer maps follow in this adult section.

AI sources: UNICEF, Guidance on AI and Children (December 2025); UNICEF Parenting, How to approach AI with children; UNESCO, Guidance for generative AI in education and research (2023). Full links, source date and limits: research/PRIMARY-1-AI-SOURCES-2026.json. These support age-appropriate adult discussion and privacy, not independent child platform use. All printed replies here are invented.

Credits: existing project fonts, established classroom/character artwork and source chapters retained without alteration; artwork hashes are in the build evidence. Counter diagrams are deterministic vector marks, not assessed AI artwork. No new generated art. Primary 2 preview: extend number work, explain addition/subtraction, compare measures and explore shapes using real materials; this is a preview, not a current-curriculum claim.

Provisional historical baseline. Current NERDC/Gombe adoption, local educator review, pupil trials, accessible-PDF certification, physical print tests and printer approval remain pending. This export is not press-ready. Independent editorial review is a separate gate.
